                                           BEFORE THE


                      LOUISIANA PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION


                                   DOCKET NUMBER U-37882




                          ENTERGY LOUISIANA, LLC, EX PARTE.




    In re: Application of Entergy Louisiana, LLC for Certification of Generation and
      Transmission Resources and for Other Relief Pursuant to the Commission ’s

                                         Lightning Initiative




                                   REPLY COMMENTS OF THE

                 LOUISIANA PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION STAFF
                           ON THE NPO MOTION FOR SUBPOENA
                                FOR PRODUCTION OF DOCUMENTS


                 The Louisiana Public Service Commission Staff (“Staff”) submits these



Reply Comments in connection with the Motion for Subpoena filed by The Alliance for

Affordable    Energy and the Union of Concerned Scientists (jointly “NPOs1”) (“NPO

Motion”) and pursuant to the “Notice of Opportunity to File Response to Subpoena For the

Production     of Documents        and   Notice   of Oral   Argument”   issued   by   the   presiding

Administrative Law          Judge (“ALJ”)    on   June   30, 2026.    After consideration     of the



Opposition of Entergy Louisiana, LLC (“ELL”) (“ELL Opposition”) ﬁled on July 2, 2026

and on further consideration of the requirements of Rule 40 of the Commission’s Rules of


Practice and Procedure, the Staff recommends                against the issuance of the subpoena



1
    Non-profit organizations.
 requested by the NPOs.                   The NPOs failed to meet the requirements of Rule 40 for each of


the ﬁve categories of document requests.


I.              THE REQUIREMENTS OF RULE 40 SHOULD BE STRICTLY APPLIED
                TO SUBPOENA REQUESTS DIRECTED TO NON-PARTY CUSTOMERS
                SEEKING SERVICE IN LOUISIANA.


                              As the Staff explained in its initial comments, the test for whether an ALJ


should grant a motion to subpoena is set forth in Rule 40 of the Commission’s Rules of


Practice and Procedure.                   That rule provides that the Commission can issue “[s]ubpoenas


for the         .   .   .   production of books, papers or documents at a hearing in a pending proceeding

                                                                                         for the issuance of
.    .   .
             upon the written motion of a party showing that there is good cause


same.”                  Rule 40   requires that a party requesting a subpoena show that the documents

requested are (1) relevant; (2) necessary; (3) will not result in unnecessary harassment,

imposition, or undue inconvenience or expense; and (4) if trade secret or confidential

treatment is requested, that there is no other alternative to accomplish the requested result.



                              As the Staff explained in its initial comments, for subpoenas directed to non-



party customers seeking new or expanded service in Louisiana, the requirements of Rule

40 should be strictly applied to ensure that the requested information is vital to the issues


before the Commission and that there is no alternative but to subpoena the information


from the customer.                     [Staff Comments    at   8].   The Commission should refrain from


expanding its regulatory reach beyond its jurisdictional utilities to prospective businesses

and individuals seeking service in Louisiana unless absolutely necessary to resolve issues


before it.                  Businesses and individuals requesting electric service in Louisiana should not
 be subject to invasive and burdensome subpoena demands absent a clear, compelling, and


speciﬁc need.


                In cases such as this one requesting certiﬁcation of new resources, it is the



regulated jurisdictional utility      that    has   the   burden   of    satisfying   the   Commission’s


certiﬁcation standards, not the customer            seeking service.      This is true      even   when the



prospective customer is causing or contributing to a certiﬁcation request of unprecedented

scale.    If the regulated utility fails to   satisfy its burden of proving that the certiﬁcation

serves   the public convenience and necessity, the request should be denied or conditioned,


as   appropriate.

                There may be situations where a subpoena to a prospective customer may be



appropriate, but this is not that situation.        The subject matters identiﬁed by the NPOs are


relevant to ELL’s Application in a broad sense, but the NPOS fail to show how the requested


information is relevant to a speciﬁc issue that they intend to raise in testimony                   or cross




examination,     or,   more   importantly,    that the    requested     information is necessary to        a




resolution of the issues before the Commission and that it is not available from another


source.    Therefore, the subpoena request should be denied for the reasons more fully


explained below.
 II.    THE NPOS FAIL TO SATISFY THEIR BURDEN OF PROVING THAT THE
       DOCUMENTS SOUGHT FROM META ARE RELEVANT, NECESSARY,
       AND         NOT      UNDULY          BURDENSOME                   PURSUANT         TO      THE

       REQUIREMENTS OF COMMISSION RULE 40.

       A.      NPO     Request No. 1   —



                                           “Analyses, Data, Calculations, and/or Evidence
               Which     Demonstrate       the          Level   of Investment   and   Permanent    Job

               Creation Expected to be Entailed By the Richland Data Center.”


               Standing alone, the wording of the NPOS’ ﬁrst request is confusing and not

as clear as Rule   40(B) requires: “Motions for subpoenas to compel the production of books,


papers, accounts or documents desired       .   .   .
                                                        shall specify as nearly as may be possible, the


books, papers, accounts or documents desired and the material and relevant facts to be


proved by them.”      LPSC Rule of Prac. & Proc. 40(B) (emphasis added).               The NPOS’ ﬁrst



request does not specify what “level of investment” it is referring to. It could be investment

in the data center, the generating and/or transmission resources to serve it, or the economy



generally.   The context of the NPO Motion suggests that this request is intended to ask for


materials related to Meta’s investment in and                   impact on the economy in and around

Richland Parish and North Louisiana, speciﬁcally including job creation.               [NPO Motion at

2-4]. Attached to the NPO Motion is a data request on this subject issued by the Alliance

for Affordable Energy (one of the NPOs) asking ELL to produce information only about


employment at the Evest data center, and not economic development investment more

generally. [Entergy Response to AAE 1-5].

               The Staff thus ﬁnds this request to be facially deﬁcient. A subpoena to a non-



party prospective     customer   (or existing           customer   seeking new service) should,   at   a




minimum, be preceded by a conventional data request to the regulated jurisdictional utility
 that asks for exactly what the      subpoena requests.        Here, the NPOs did not ask for the


speciﬁc data it is requesting in a data request to ELL.

                Moving beyond       this   facial    deﬁciency,    the   subpoena request          is   also



substantively deﬁcient under the Rule 40 standards. Interpreting the request as a request

for economic      development investment and job creation associated with the Evest data

center and    applying Rule 40 requirements to it, the Staff concludes that although the

economic     development impact information requested is relevant, it is not necessary to

resolve the issues before the Commission. ELL’s application seeks a Commission finding


that the proposed investments “serve the public convenience and necessity and is in the


public interest, and    is therefore   prudent,     in accordance with the Commission’s                 1983


General Order.”      [ELL Application at 27].             The Commission    can   consider economic



development benefits in its broad view of “public interest,” but it is not required to.                 The


Commission’s primary interest is in ensuring that electric rates for all customers are just


and reasonable and that other customers are not forced to pay for resources that are properly


attributable to   serving Meta.   This requires      an   analysis of the cost of the resources and

Meta’s contribution to those costs         through the various      mechanisms      presented in the

application, and the likely rate impact on other customers.

                If the Commission goes beyond that to examine the wider economic benefits


from a customer’s proposed project or expansion, it can rely on public sources and reports


or   on   general knowledge   and    logical reasoning       about the   likely impact of the core

investment    directly to the project proposed by the customer,             as   well   as   the   utility’s

investment in the resources to serve it. While potentially helpful, it is not necessary for the



                                                    -5-
     Commission to have economic development data from the customer for its public interest


    ﬁnding.

                       Although     the   Staff recommends      against issuing    a   subpoena   for   this



.
    information, ELL should produce any information it has on this subject as soon as possible.

    In its Opposition, ELL suggests that economic development should be a factor supporting


    its   application:     “[T]he Company is conﬁdent that the publicly available information

    concerning Meta’s substantial investment in Louisiana            —
                                                                         both as to the numbers that have


    been reported and the ongoing transformation that all Louisianians can see happening in


    the northeast region of our state        —




                                                 support certification of the resources proposed in this


    matter.”      [ELL Opposition at 10]. Since ELL has the burden of proof in this matter, if it

    has anything in its possession, or is aware of any reports on the economic impact of Meta’s


    investment in the Evest data center beyond what is cited on pages 12-13 of Phillip May’s


    Direct Testimony (which primarily relates to Laidley investment), it should identify those


    materials     as   soon as   possible if it wants the Commission to consider them in its public

    interest analysis. The Staff has been unable to independently locate any public reports on


    the incremental economic development impact of the Evest data center.


             B.        NPO   Request No. 2       “Analyses, Data, Reports, Calculations, and/or
                                                  —




                       Evidence     Which    Substantiate the Amount of Electricity Load the
                       Richland Data Center Will Need.”


                       The NPOs      allege that ELL has “declined to provide any documentation,

    analyses, or studies that support the Customer’s need for a specific amount of power,

    instead pointing to the demand level that the Customer has contracted for.”            [NPO Motion

    at 4]. The NPOs claim that “[i]nformation about the electric load required by the proposed




                                                         -6-
 Richland Data Center is crucial to         assess       the    magnitude of new generating capacity

required to be built or procured” and requests that the ALJ issue a subpoena to Meta

ordering the company to provide additional evidence to substantiate its electricity load

projections. [Id at 6]. Although the Staff agrees with the NPOs that the amount of electric

load that Evest will require for its new data center is an important consideration, the Staff


does not agree that ELL has “declined to provide” sufﬁcient information to support the


load   requirement   claimed   by   Meta   or   that        additional,   more   detailed information is



“necessary” to adjudicate this proceeding.


               In the ELL Opposition, ELL explains that the ESA is “a binding contract for


a   specified amount of load,” which demonstrates, on its own, “the Customer’s need for

purposes of the Company’s resource planning.”                 [ELL Opposition at 11]. Staff agrees. The

fact that Evest has contracted for a certain amount of load and agreed to pay the full revenue


requirement for the generators needed to supply that load during the term of the ESA,

provides substantial evidence that the new Evest data center will require the load that ELL

and Evest claim is needed.     [See Direct Testimony of Laura Beauchamp (AEO) at 38; LKB-

2 (AEO) at 2; LKB—3 (AEO) at 84 (Customer Questionnaire)].


               ELL witness Thomas Kidd testiﬁes that the Minimum                       Monthly Charges


(“MMCS”) that Evest will pay under the ESA will cover the entire revenue requirement of

the seven new generating units for the 20-year term of the contract.                [Direct Testimony of

Thomas Kidd at 7 (“As set forth in the ESA.         .   .
                                                            the Company and the Customer have agreed


that these monthly minimum charges will fully recover the revenue requirement during the
 term   of the ESA of both the ELL-Funded Transmission              Project and the generation and

capacity     resources   being constructed     in   connection    with   the   Customer’s   load.”)].


Moreover, the MMCs that Evest agreed to pay reﬂect an accelerated 20-year depreciable


life for the four      Proposed   Generators to be located in Richland Parish,         resulting   in



approximately 90% of those four generators being depreciated during the initial ESA term.

[Direct Testimony of Ryan Jones at 16].

                The Staff’ s analysis of this is on-going, but the ESA also contains termination


                                                                                                ELL
provisions that appear to provide significant cost coverage for unused generators.

witness Phillip May states:       “[T]he Customer has agreed that it will pay, in the event of an

early termination of the ESA and following a specified liquidation process, the remaining

net book value of any Proposed Generators that are in service and that the Company does



not retain for general    supply purposes.” [Direct Testimony of Phillip May at 34].          These


termination provisions further decrease the likelihood that Evest would have contracted for


megawatts it does not need.

                The NPOs do not provide any plausible theory as to why Evest would enter


into   an   ESA that   requires it to pay for generators, some with accelerated depreciation

payments, that it does not anticipate needing to operate its data center. It is true that other


ratepayers would be required to pay for any remaining costs of the generators after 20 years


if Evest does not        renew   the ESA.    But that is   a   risk that will be factored into the


Commission’s public interest determination and that risk assessment will not be aided by


additional information supplied by Meta on Evest’s load requirements. The NPOS’ request
 to subpoena Meta for “the amount of electricity load the Richland data center will need”



should be denied as unnecessary to the adjudication of this proceeding.


        C.      NPO  Request No. 3    “Analyses, Data, Reports, Calculations, and/or
                                         —




                Evidence Providing the Richland Data Center’s Load Factor and

                Expected Variability Over Time Including Daily, Weekly, and Monthly
                Load Variability.”


                The NPOs allege in their motion that “ELL claimed that the Customer will


have an ‘around-the-clock’ energy usage profile” but “relies on bare assertions from the


Customer of its intended or expected power factor.”              [NPO Motion at 4].      NPOs claim that


ELL’s    responses    to   data   requests    on    this   are   deficient   because    it     “provided   no




documentation     from the Customer”          and    instead “referred back”       to    its    own   “Excel



workpaper.” [NPO Motion at 5].          The NPOs provide only a one—sentence explanation of



why more information directly from the Customer is needed, and it is the same explanation

they give for NPO Request No. 2: “[I]nformation about the electric load required by the

proposed Richland Data Center is crucial to assess the magnitude of new generating

capacity required to be built or procured.” [Id. at 6]. For the same reasons expressed above,

the load factor information is not “necessary” for the “assess[ment] of the magnitude of


new   generating capacity required.”         The Customer’s contracted load, minimum payment



obligations, and early termination provisions are definitive evidence of the Customer’s load

requirements.

                In addition, production of load factor data from the Customer by subpoena is


not necessary because ELL has provided data regarding the Customer’s load factor. As the



ELL   Opposition points out, the Customer provided its load factor in its Transmission
 Questionnaire attached as Exhibit H to the CIAC Agreement, which is provided in pre-ﬁled

exhibit LKB-3.        In   addition, ELL provided detailed load information in its response to

Staff-ELL data request 1-66.          [ELL Opposition at 11].         ELL also referenced these two



pieces of information in response to Alliance for Affordable Energy data request 3-l5(c),

which is attached to the NPO Motion.


         D.        NPO     Request No.   4   —
                                                 “A
                                              Copy or Records of Any Communication
                   Between Meta and ELL Discussing the Sustainability Agreement as a
                   Relevant Factor For the Customer in Deciding to Move Forward With

                   Building a Data Center in Louisiana.”

                   The NPOs request that the ALJ issue            a   subpoena to Meta ordering the

company       to   produce   all   communications       between   Meta    and   ELL   that   discuss   the


Sustainability Agreement as a relevant factor for Evest deciding to build its data center in

Louisiana.     [NPO Motion at 8]. As an initial matter, this request should be denied because

it is unduly burdensome under Rule 40, which provides that the subpoena request must


“not result in unnecessary harassment,           imposition, or undue inconvenience or expense.”

LPSC Rule of Prac. & Proc. 40(B).            NPOs request that a subpoena be issued to Meta, a



nonparty to this proceeding, for communications “between Meta and ELL,” even though


ELL is a party to the proceeding. ELL should be in possession of the same communications


as   Meta that would be responsive to the request.           The NPOS do not explain how it is not


unduly burdensome to subpoena documents from Meta when ELL has possession of those

same   communications.


                   The proper means for the NPOs to obtain those communications would be to


request them from ELL, the regulated utility under the jurisdiction of the Commission, in




                                                      -10-
 the normal course of discovery, not through a subpoena to a nonparty prospective utility


customer. The Staff has not found any request for communications between ELL and Meta



through discovery directed to ELL.          The NPOS’ Motion cites to Data Request AAE 2-13,


but that request asks ELL only to “provide the sustainability goals of the Customer (or its



corporate affiliates);” it did not   request communications between          ELL and Meta regarding

Request 2- 13 (included in Attachment A of NPOs’ Motion)].

                 The NPOS’ request for communications regarding Meta’s sustainability goals


should also be denied because it fails to satisfy the requirement of Rule 40 that information


be necessary to resolve a proceeding before a subpoena can be issued.               The Staff agrees


that     information   concerning    the   Sustainability Agreement     is   generally   relevant and


information that aids understanding of the specific provisions at issue would be helpful to


adjudicate those provisions.         However, the NPOs’ subpoena motion does               not   request

request information “discussing the Sustainability Agreement as a relevant factor for the

Customer in deciding to move forward with building a data center in Louisiana.”                  [Motion

at 8].



                 'We%ammNkmmmELLmwmdmmasmmmwmwﬁgmmwmamhm

provisions contained in that agreement are distinct from information regarding why Meta

chose to build its data center in Louisiana.             Meta’s motivation for     entering into the

Sustainability Agreement or any other contract is not necessary for a fair adjudication of

this   proceeding.     Furthermore, ELL does       not    ask for   approval   of the    Sustainability


                                                 -11-
 Agreement as the NPOs allege. [NPO Motion at 2]. Instead, ELL seeks approval of only

certain aspects of the Sustainability Agreement; Meta’s sustainability goals and/or what it


may have communicated with ELL about the Sustainability Agreement are not relevant to


whether these provisions are in the public interest.


                 The     Staff also    agrees    with      ELL’s    assertions   that   the    “Sustainability

Agreement itself proves the Customer’s commitments to sustainability.” [ELL Opposition

at   12].   In its response to data request AAE 2-13, ELL also provides a citation to Meta’s



publicly     available    corporate sustainability goals that show Meta’s intent regarding


sustainability and clean energy, including a link to Meta’s 2025 Sustainability Report.

Meta’s goals set forth in that 73-page report are consistent with the provisions contained in


the ELL Sustainability Agreement.


                 The 2025       Sustainability Report explains, among other things, Meta’s clean

and renewable energy goals, policies, and history of clean energy successes. It states:


                 For     more   than   a   decade,    we      have reduced   emissions        by
                 ensuring   our   operations    are   supported by clean and renewable
                 energy.    We recognize that adding new energy capacity to the

                 grid is important, not only because of our scale and scope as a
                 company, but because we want to play a positive role in the
                 communities in which we operate.


                 Since 2020, we have matched 100% of our annual electricity
                 use with clean and renewable energy.             As a voluntary buyer, we

                 prioritize supporting high quality, innovative energy projects
                 around the globe, which is key to maintaining net zero
                 emissions for our operations.


                 A fundamental tenet of our approach to clean and renewable

                 energy is the concept of additionality: partnering with utilities
                 and developers to add new projects to the grid.             Over the last

                 decade, we have contracted for over 15 GW of new clean and



                                                       -12-
               renewable energy     across    the
                                             globe, making us           one   of the
              world’s largest corporate buyers.


Meta, 2025 Sustainability Report at 18, available at https://sustainability.atmeta.com/ (last

visited July 6, 2026). It is unclear what additional information the NPOs believe would be


contained in communications between ELL and Meta that is “necessary” to adjudicate this


proceeding.

       E.     NPO    Request No.     5   —

                                             “Information    on   the   Location, Amount, and
              Nature of Assets Held by Meta Platforms, Inc. Sufficient to Fulfill Its
              Obligations Under the Guaranty, and Information on Other Guaranties
              Meta has Made to Other Electric Utilities.”


              The Staff agrees with the NPOs that the ﬁnancial viability of Meta is          a




relevant and important issue, but a broad—ranging subpoena for the “location, amount, and


nature of assets held by Meta Platforms, Inc” is not necessary for a determination of issues



presented in this proceeding.   Indeed, the subpoena is more likely to unduly harass and

inconvenience the Customer than it is to lead to data that would be usable and probative in


this proceeding.


              Information regarding Meta’s ﬁnancial metrics and health are already in the


public domain in Meta’s public ﬁlings with the Security and Exchange Commission

(“SEC”), and in Meta’s credit ratings assigned by recognized credit rating agencies.      The


NPOs do not explain why they need more information than the SEC requires or suggest


there is something missing from Meta’s SEC ﬁlings. The NPOs do not suggest, nor can it



reasonably be expected, that they, the Commission, or any witness in this case could

assemble, analyze and interpret the requested asset data and come to a sound conclusion

that would be reliable   or more   accurate than      ﬁnancial analyses that have already been




                                               -13-
 performed by rating agencies Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s (“S&P”) and that have been

discussed in Entergy’s pre-filed testimony.


                 ELL witness Thomas Kidd explains the importance of the S&P and Moody’s


credit ratings to ELL’s overall analysis of the Evest project in his direct testimony:


                 [C]redit rating agencies such as Moody’s Ratings (“Moody’s”)
                 and S&P Global Ratings (“S&P”) assign ratings by assessing
                 financial   information   toanalyze leverage, liquidity, and
                 proﬁtability metrics. Of particular interest to these rating
                 agencies for regulated utilities are the various credit ratios,
                 specifically the ratio between Cash Flow from Operations
                 before Changes in Working Capital (“CFO pre-WC”) to Debt
                 evaluated by Moody’s and the ratio between Funds from

                 Operations (“FFO”) to Debt evaluated by S&P (collectively,
                 the “Key Credit Ratios”). Rating agencies use metrics like the

                 Key Credit Ratios to evaluate whether a utility’s cash ﬂow
                 from operations is sufficient to service its debt. These metrics
                 and   a   variety of other factors, including regulatory
                 environment, are evaluated by the rating agencies to establish
                 thresholds below which     Company is at risk for a credit
                                                a

                 downgrade, which in turn impacts the amount of and terms by
                 which the Company can borrow money, affecting both ELL
                 and its customers.


[Direct Testimony of Thomas Kidd at 12].

                 ELL witness Mr. Hinkson testifies that Meta’s current credit rating is AA-
                                                                                                     by

S&P and Aa3 by Moody’s.          [Direct Testimony of Kenroy Hinkson at 8]. That testimony

supports ELL’s comments that S&P and Moody’s credit ratings show that “Meta has the


ﬁnancial wherewithal to support the Customer’s obligations in this matter, should the need


ever   arise.”   [ELL Opposition at 12].            It is not reasonable   or   efﬁcient to expect the


Commission or any party in this case to conduct its own forensic accounting review of


Meta’s assets to determine Meta’s credit worthiness in order to certify                resources   when




                                                     -14-
 rating agencies with extensive expertise have already conducted that analysis.      The value


of any such forensic accounting review conducted in the context of this proceeding would


not likely lead to valuable evidence in any event.



                 Importantly, the ESA also includes a liquid collateral security mechanism

that addresses these issues.    If there are any    signs that Meta is struggling or may soon

struggle ﬁnancially, that information would be reﬂected in its credit rating and trigger

liquid collateral to be paid by Meta as security. If Meta’s credit rating were to ever drop to

certain ratings as speciﬁed in the ESA, the customer would be required to contribute a


certain amount of the Meta Guaranty in cash or letter of credit.    [See LKB-2 (AEO) at 46-

47].

                 Additionally, Meta discloses ﬁnancial data on an annual basis under SEC

rules. As ELL points out, Meta’s most recent Form 10-K ﬁled in January 2026 “discloses


a   balance sheet with more than $366 billion in assets and revenues of nearly $201 billion


in 2025.”      [ELL Opposition at 12].   The NPOs do not challenge the accuracy of these


disclosures.    Meta’s credit ratings and SEC ﬁlings are the best evidence of Meta’s ability


to satisfy its obligations under the guaranty if ever called upon to do so.   The combination


of the signiﬁcant collateral   security provided by the ESA and the ﬁnancial information

already   in the   public   domain render the NPOS’       subpoena request    for Meta’s   asset



information unnecessary.




                                             -15-
               F.         Miscellaneous Issues Raised in the ELL Opposition.


                         1.     NPOs’ failed to verify their motion for subpoena in accordance
                                with Rule 40 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and
                                Procedure.


                         The Louisiana Code of Civil Procedure states that “[p]leadings need not be


verified          or   accompanied by affidavit or certiﬁcate, except as otherwise provided by

law   .   .   .
                  .”   La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 863   (emphasis added).             Rule 40 ofthe Commission’s


Rules of Practice and Procedure provides an exception to that general rule. Rule 40 is clear


that a motion for the Commission to issue a subpoena must be verified.                                         LPSC Rule of


Prac. & Proc. 40(B) (“Motions for subpoenas                  .   .   .
                                                                         shall be veriﬁed    .   .   .
                                                                                                         .” (emphasis added)).


Thus, under Rule 40 ofthe Commission’s Rules and Article 863 ofthe Louisiana Code of

Civil Procedure, the NPOs’ motion was deficient because it did not include a verification.


The Staff notes that the NPOs ﬁled a verified motion on July 6, 2026 to cure that defect.


                         ELL claims that the NPOS’ failure to                  verify    its motion “alone           justiﬁes

denying the Motion outright.” [ELL Opposition at 8]. The Staff does not opine on whether

the NPO Motion should be denied on the basis of this technical deﬁciency, now rectiﬁed.


Instead, pursuant to the comments above, the Staff believes that the NPOs’ Motion should

be denied based on the merits of its requests and the substantive requirements that must be


satisfied for the issuance of a subpoena under Rule 40.


                         2.     Hearsay    evidence     is           admissible         in    hearings           before   the
                                Commission.


                         NPOs allege that “[w]ithout Meta sponsoring its own declarations” regarding


the issues central to the           subpoena request, “the assertions by ELL are hearsay and thus




                                                        -15-
 inadmissible.”   [NPO Motion at 7]. Staff disagrees. Contrary to NPOs’ assertions, hearsay

evidence is allowed in administrative     proceedings and experts are allowed to rely on

hearsay evidence.    ELL correctly cites Rule 32 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and


Procedure and concludes that “evidence beyond that which is admissible under the rules of


evidence can be admissible in proceedings before the Commission.          [ELL Opposition at 15


(emphasis in original)].

                Whether ELL relies on hearsay as a primary source of evidence for certain


issues should go to the weight of the evidence and whether ELL has sufficiently supported


its   application, but that evidence is not prohibited at hearings before the Commission.

Quoting    the Louisiana First Circuit Court of Appeal, the Commission              explained    in


Louisiana Public Service Comm ’n v. Classic Formalwear & Limousine Services, No. T-


30039, 2007 WL 4128255, at *6 (Aug. 23, 2007) that although admissible in Commission


proceedings, hearsay evidence is not competent evidence that can prove a case.                  Id.



(“Hearsay evidence is admissible at administrative hearings, but it is well settled that

hearsay evidence is not competent evidence, and it is competent evidence that proves the

case.”). Although ELL is correct that hearsay evidence is admissible, its reliance on that

evidence is at its own peril when it carries the burden of proof.


III.     CONCLUSION


                The NPOs    motion   fails to   satisfy   the   requirements   of Rule 40   of the


Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure and should be denied in full.
